result: HIV-Tg rats exhibit selective cognitive deficits in attentional set-shifting but not in position discrimination or reversal learning. HIV-Tg rats performed significantly worse than WT controls in the shift to cue phase, with only 4/6 animals reaching criterion and taking significantly longer to complete the task (949.5±146.3 vs 350.8±84 TTC).
evaluation: Claims C26-C31 provide converging behavioral evidence showing selective impairment in set-shifting in HIV-Tg rats. The data include trials to criterion, proportion reaching criterion, and linear regression analysis of learning rates (F(1,11)=15.94, p=0.0021), all supporting the conclusion of selective cognitive dysfunction in the mPFC-mediated task.

result: HIV-Tg rats show reduced dendritic spine density in layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the mPFC with a shift from mature (thin and mushroom) to immature (stubby) spine morphology. Overall spine density, thin spine density, and mushroom spine density were all significantly reduced, while stubby spine density was increased.
evaluation: Claims C32-C36 demonstrate consistent structural deficits in HIV-Tg rats using DiOlistic labeling and Neurolucida 360 analysis. The morphological shift from mature to immature spines is well-documented with quantitative data (Figure 2A-D), providing strong evidence for synaptic pathology in the HIV-Tg model.

result: Dendritic spine density in the mPFC correlates specifically with set-shifting performance but not with position discrimination or reversal learning. The correlation is stronger when considering only thin spine density (Pearson's r=-0.7920, p=0.0063) compared to overall spine density (Pearson's r=-0.7368, p=0.0151).
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 establish a specific structure-function relationship between mPFC spine density and cognitive flexibility. The selective correlation with set-shifting but not other behavioral phases (C39-C40) supports the anatomical specificity of the deficit and strengthens the link between thin spines and cognitive flexibility.

result: ICV administration of CXCL12 rescues cognitive flexibility deficits in HIV-Tg rats. CXCL12-treated rats took significantly fewer trials to reach criterion (701.3±97.26 vs 1191±114.5 TTC), more animals completed the task (7/10 vs 2/9), and reached criterion at a faster rate (F(1,16)=44.3781, p<0.001). Long-term CXCL12 treatment showed no deleterious effects in WT rats.
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 demonstrate robust behavioral rescue by CXCL12 with multiple convergent measures (trials to criterion, completion rate, learning rate). The inclusion of WT controls (C45) showing no adverse effects strengthens the therapeutic potential. Statistical analyses are appropriate and effect sizes are substantial.

result: CXCL12 treatment completely restores dendritic spine density and morphology in HIV-Tg rats. CXCL12 significantly increased overall spine density and thin spine density while decreasing stubby spine density, with no changes in mushroom spines or filopodia. Spine density in CXCL12-treated HIV-Tg rats was not significantly different from vehicle-treated WT rats.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 demonstrate complete structural rescue by CXCL12, with spine density returning to WT levels (C50). The specific effects on thin and stubby spines (C47-C48) align with the proposed mechanism of spine maturation. The lack of effect on mushroom spines (C49) is consistent with their stability and provides specificity to the findings.

result: In CXCL12-treated HIV-Tg rats, spine density correlates with cognitive performance, with thin spine density showing a stronger relationship (Pearson's r=-0.8493, p=0.0038) than overall spine density (Pearson's r=-0.7676, p=0.0157) with trials to criterion in set-shifting.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 establish that the structural rescue by CXCL12 correlates with functional recovery. The stronger correlation with thin spines specifically supports the hypothesis that thin spine restoration drives cognitive improvement. The correlation analyses are appropriately conducted and reported.

result: CXCL12 activates Rac1 in cultured cortical neurons with a time-dependent increase in Rac1-GTP levels at 5 and 15 minutes, returning to baseline by 30 minutes, without altering total Rac1 levels.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 demonstrate CXCL12-induced Rac1 activation using a standard PAK1 pulldown assay with appropriate positive and negative controls (Figure 4A). The time course is well-characterized and the lack of change in total Rac1 (C59) confirms specificity for the GTP-bound active form.

result: CXCL12-induced Rac1 activation requires CXCR4 and Gαi signaling. Pretreatment with the CXCR4 antagonist AMD3100 or pertussis toxin (PTX) completely blocked CXCL12-induced Rac1 activation.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 establish the receptor and G-protein dependence of CXCL12 signaling using pharmacological inhibitors. The complete blockade by both AMD3100 and PTX provides strong evidence for CXCR4/Gαi-mediated signaling. C62 is supported by citation to prior work (Pitcher et al., 2014).

result: CXCL12 activates the Rac1/PAK/LIMK1/cofilin signaling cascade in cortical neurons. CXCL12 treatment resulted in time-dependent phosphorylation of PAK1, LIMK1, and cofilin, which was completely blocked by inhibition of CXCR4 or Gαi signaling. CXCL12 also increased phosphorylation of SSH1 after one hour.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 demonstrate activation of the complete Rac1 downstream signaling pathway using Western blot analysis with phospho-specific antibodies (Figure 5A-D). The pharmacological blockade experiments (C64-C65) confirm pathway specificity. The SSH1 phosphorylation data (C66) reveals dual regulation of cofilin activity.

result: CXCL12 treatment shifts the F/G-actin ratio toward F-actin polymerization. Cortical neurons treated with CXCL12 for 1-2 hours showed a four-fold increase in F/G-actin ratio compared to vehicle controls.
evaluation: Claim C67 provides functional evidence that Rac1/PAK pathway activation leads to increased actin polymerization. The F/G-actin fractionation assay includes appropriate controls (latrunculin A and jaspakinolide) and the four-fold increase represents a substantial effect size (Figure 5E).

result: CXCL12 specifically increases thin spine density while reducing stubby spine density in cultured cortical neurons after 3 hours of treatment.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 demonstrate that CXCL12 effects on actin polymerization translate to specific morphological changes in dendritic spines. The increase in thin spines with concurrent decrease in stubby spines suggests spine maturation, consistent with the in vivo findings and the proposed mechanism.

result: Pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 with NSC23766 completely blocks CXCL12-induced Rac1 activation, downstream signaling, and spine density changes in cultured neurons. NSC23766 alone had no effect on spine density or morphology.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 establish Rac1 as essential for CXCL12 effects using the specific inhibitor NSC23766. The complete blockade of Rac1 activation (C70), downstream signaling (C71), and spine changes (C72) provides strong evidence for pathway specificity. The negative control (C73) confirms no off-target effects of acute Rac1 inhibition.

result: Genetic knockdown of Rac1 using shRNA prevents CXCL12-mediated modulation of spine density and morphology. Prolonged Rac1 knockdown reduced total spine density in both vehicle and CXCL12-treated neurons.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 provide genetic validation of Rac1 requirement using shRNA knockdown. The inability of CXCL12 to modulate spines in Rac1 knockdown neurons (C74) confirms the pharmacological findings. The baseline reduction in spine density with prolonged knockdown (C75) is consistent with prior literature (Tashiro and Yuste, 2004).

result: CXCL12 treatment increases pPAK1 levels in NeuN+ neurons in the mPFC of both WT and HIV-Tg rats. Basal pPAK1 levels were lower in HIV-Tg neurons compared to WT, and CXCL12 treatment restored pPAK1 to baseline levels in HIV-Tg animals.
evaluation: Claims C76-C78 demonstrate in vivo activation of the Rac1/PAK pathway using immunohistochemistry and multispectral imaging (Figure 7A). The finding of reduced basal pPAK1 in HIV-Tg rats (C77) provides mechanistic insight into the spine deficits, and the restoration by CXCL12 (C78) links pathway activation to therapeutic effects.

result: pPAK1 levels in cortical neurons correlate positively with dendritic spine density (Pearson's r=0.5602, p=0.0372) and negatively with trials to criterion in set-shifting (Pearson's r=-0.5526, p=0.048).
evaluation: Claims C79-C80 establish that PAK1 activation correlates with both structural and functional outcomes across all experimental groups. The correlations link the molecular mechanism to spine density and cognitive performance, supporting the proposed pathway as the mediator of CXCL12 effects.

result: Total Rac1 protein levels are unchanged between WT and HIV-Tg rats, but untreated HIV-Tg rats have reduced levels of active Rac1-GTP compared to WT animals.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 demonstrate that the deficit in HIV-Tg rats is due to reduced Rac1 activation rather than reduced Rac1 expression. This finding is consistent with the pPAK1 data (C77) and provides mechanistic insight into the pathology. The pulldown assay from PFC tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) provides direct evidence.

result: ICV administration of NSC23766 dose-dependently reduces Rac1 activation and pPAK1 levels in the frontal cortex in vivo, validating the approach for behavioral studies.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 establish that NSC23766 effectively inhibits Rac1 signaling in vivo at the doses used for behavioral experiments. The dose-dependent effects on both Rac1-GTP (C83) and pPAK1 (C84) provide validation for the subsequent behavioral and structural studies with Rac1 inhibition.

result: In vivo Rac1 inhibition with NSC23766 prevents CXCL12-mediated improvements in cognitive flexibility and dendritic spine changes in WT rats. NSC23766 blocked both the behavioral improvement and the structural changes in overall spine density, thin spine density, and stubby spine density.
evaluation: Claims C85-C87 demonstrate that Rac1 activation is necessary for CXCL12 effects in vivo using pharmacological inhibition. The blockade of both behavioral (C85) and structural (C86-C87) improvements provides strong evidence that Rac1 mediates CXCL12 therapeutic effects in physiological conditions.

result: In WT rats treated with NSC23766, spine density correlates with set-shifting performance, with the correlation being stronger for thin spine density (Pearson's r=-0.8350, p=0.0058) than overall spine density (Pearson's r=-0.7862, p=0.0121).
evaluation: Claims C88-C89 show that the structure-function relationship is maintained even when Rac1 is inhibited, supporting the central role of thin spines in cognitive flexibility. The correlations across all four treatment groups strengthen the generalizability of the spine-cognition relationship.

result: NSC23766 blocks CXCL12-mediated recovery of dendritic spine density and morphology in HIV-Tg rats, preventing increases in overall and thin spine density and decreases in stubby spine density.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 demonstrate that Rac1 activation is necessary for CXCL12 therapeutic effects in the disease model. The blockade of structural recovery by NSC23766 in HIV-Tg rats parallels the findings in WT rats and confirms that the same mechanism operates in both physiological and pathological conditions.

result: In HIV-Tg rats treated with NSC23766, thin spine density shows a strong negative correlation with set-shifting performance (Pearson's r=-0.7787, p=0.0029), while overall spine density does not correlate significantly (Pearson's r=-0.2256, p=0.4808).
evaluation: Claims C94-C95 show an unexpected dissociation between overall and thin spine density correlations in the HIV-Tg NSC23766 groups. While the thin spine correlation (C95) is consistent with other findings, the lack of overall spine density correlation (C94) is unexplained and may reflect limited sample size (n=12) or treatment-specific effects. This warrants further investigation.

result: CXCL12 depends on Rac1 activation to drive improvements in cognitive flexibility and dendritic spine number in both physiological and neuroinflammatory conditions.
evaluation: Claim C96 is a summary conclusion supported by the combined pharmacological inhibition studies in both WT (C85-C89) and HIV-Tg (C91-C95) rats. The consistency of Rac1 requirement across both genotypes and for both behavioral and structural outcomes provides strong support for this conclusion.

result: The selective impairment in set-shifting but not position discrimination or reversal learning in HIV-Tg rats indicates region-specific neuronal injury, consistent with the known role of the mPFC (particularly PrL) in mediating strategy shifting.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 provide appropriate interpretation of the behavioral findings in the context of established neuroanatomy. The citations to Birrell and Brown, 2000; Floresco et al., 2008 (C98) and Hamilton and Brigman, 2015 (C99) support the anatomical specificity of the deficits and justify the focus on mPFC for structural analyses.

result: This is the first study to demonstrate complete recovery of both structural and behavioral deficits in the HIV-Tg rat model, with studies conducted at an age where animals were already impaired, demonstrating reversibility of dendritic spine injury and cognitive dysfunction.
evaluation: Claims C104-C105 assert novelty and reversibility of the findings. The complete restoration of spine density to WT levels (C50) and behavioral recovery (C42-C44) in animals with pre-existing deficits support the reversibility claim. The novelty claim appears justified based on the literature review, though comprehensive verification would require extensive literature search.

result: Restoring thin spines is a key driver of cognitive function mediated by the mPFC, representing the first report of this phenomenon in a rodent model of HAND.
evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are supported by the stronger correlations between thin spine density and cognitive performance compared to overall spine density (C38, C52, C89, C95). The specific increase in thin spines by CXCL12 (C47, C68) coupled with behavioral improvement provides evidence for this conclusion. The novelty claim appears reasonable.

result: The Rac1/PAK pathway mediates CXCL12 effects on actin polymerization in cortical neurons, with CXCL12 acting on multiple pathway components (PAK1/LIMK1 and SSH1) to regulate cofilin phosphorylation. Rac1 activation is the exclusive mediator of CXCL12 effects on spine density and morphology.
evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by the comprehensive mechanistic studies showing Rac1 activation (C57-C61), downstream signaling (C63-C66), functional actin changes (C67), and complete blockade by Rac1 inhibition/knockdown (C70-C75). The dual regulation of cofilin through both LIMK1 and SSH1 (C111) is well-documented. The claim of novelty in cortical neurons (C109) appears justified.

result: Rac1 inhibition had no effects on position discrimination or reversal learning, suggesting specificity for mPFC-mediated functions. This represents the first study connecting Rac1 activation with behavioral flexibility.
evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by behavioral data showing no effects of NSC23766 on the first two task phases (Figure 8—figure supplement 3, Figure 9—figure supplement 1). This specificity strengthens the mPFC-specific role of Rac1 in set-shifting. The novelty claim (C113) regarding Rac1 and behavioral flexibility appears reasonable, though the authors appropriately note this warrants further investigation.

result: These findings suggest therapeutic potential for targeting CXCR4 agonists or Rac1/PAK signaling pathways for neurorestorative therapies in HAND and other diseases characterized by spine loss, with small molecule CXCR4 agonists now available for preclinical studies.
evaluation: Claims C130-C133 represent appropriate speculation about therapeutic implications based on the complete rescue of structural and behavioral deficits. The suggestion of CXCR4 agonists (C131) is supported by the data, and the citation of available small molecule agonists (C133, Mishra et al., 2016) provides a path forward. These are reasonable translational conclusions from the findings.
